--- lecture: "b" metadata-files: - ../../_slide-settings.yml format: revealjs: theme: default --- ::: {.t-title} ::: {.t-eyebrow} {{< meta course >}} ::: # Importing & Exploring ::: {.t-rule} ::: ::: {.t-meta} Unit {{< meta unit >}} · Chapter {{< meta chapter >}} · Lecture {{< meta chapter >}}{{< meta lecture >}} ::: ::: {.t-attrib} {{< meta attribution >}} ::: ![]({{< meta unit-art >}}){.t-art} ::: ## Roadmap: More Programming ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} 1. Data Frames 2. Data Files 3. Data Exploration ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/map.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: # Data Frames ## Tidy Data {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - There are many ways to store data ::: {.fragment .mt1} - We will be learning the [tidy data]{.b .blue} format - Data should be *rectangular* - Each [variable]{.green} has its own column - Each [observation]{.green} has its own row - Each [value]{.green} has its own cell ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} ![](../../img/tidydata.png) ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/spreadsheet.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Other Data Advice {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - [Name all variables]{.b .blue} in the first row - This is called a [header row]{.b .green} ::: {.fragment .mt1} - [Avoid merged cells]{.b .blue} for data storage - These are okay for communication ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - [Avoid empty cells]{.b .blue} whenever possible - Mark [missing data]{.b .green} as `NA` ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - [Avoid formatting-as-data]{.b .blue} for storage - e.g., non-redundant color-coding ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/light_bulb.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Tidying Example 1 {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="45%"} #### Not Tidy
Name Ann Bob Cat Dom
Age 13 10 11 11
Weight 56.4 46.8 41.3 43.3
::: {.fragment .mt1 .pv4} ❌ Here, each row is a variable and each column is an observation. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="10%"} ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.fragment} #### Tidy
Name Age Weight
Ann 13 56.4
Bob 10 46.8
Cat 11 41.3
Dom 11 43.3
::: {.pv4} ✔️ Here, each column is a variable and each row is an observation. ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Tidying Example 2 {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="45%"} #### Not Tidy
Names: Ann Bob Cat Dom
Age Weight
13 56.4
10 46.8
11 41.3
11 43.3
::: {.fragment .mt1 .pv4} ❌ Here, we have data that is not rectangular because the Names variable has its own row. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="10%"} ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.fragment} #### Tidy
Name Age Weight
Ann 13 56.4
Bob 10 46.8
Cat 11 41.3
Dom 11 43.3
::: {.pv4} ✔️ Here, we have made the data rectangular by moving the Names variable to its own column. ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Tidying Example 3 {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="45%"} #### Not Tidy
country year cases / population
Afghanistan 1999 NA / 19987071
2000 2666 / 20595360
Brazil 1999 37737 / 172006362
2000 80488 / 174504898
China 1999 212258 / 1272915272
2000 213766 / 1280428583
::: {.fragment .mt1 .pv4} ❌ Here, we have merged cells and two values stored in a single cell. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="10%"} ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.fragment} #### Tidy
country year cases population
Afghanistan 1999 NA 19987071
Afghanistan 2000 2666 20595360
Brazil 1999 37737 172006362
Brazil 2000 80488 174504898
China 1999 212258 1272915272
China 2000 213766 1280428583
::: {.pv4} ✔️ Here, we have un-merged the countries and separated the cases and populations variables into columns. ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Tibbles {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - R works particularly well with [tidy data]{.b .green} ::: {.fragment .mt1} - We store tidy data in [data frames]{.b .green} or [tibbles]{.b .blue} - Tibbles are just fancier data frames
(i.e., they have a few extra features) ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - To use tibbles, we need the [tidyverse]{.b .blue} package ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - Tibbles are constructed from one or more vectors - The vectors must have the [same length]{.b .green} - They can contain [different types]{.b .green} of data ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/new_train.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Parallel Vectors {.fs70} ![](../../img/vectors.png) ::: {.tc .pv4} We start with three separate vector objects that all have the same length. We set it up so that the $n$-th car in each train corresponds to the same observation. ::: ## Tibble {.fs70} ![](../../img/tibble.png) ::: {.tc .pv4} Then we combine the vectors into a single tibble (or data frame) object. Now, as the tibble moves around, the variables always stay together. ::: ## Loading the tidyverse Install it once via [Extras pane > Packages tab > Install]{.b .blue}, then load it each session. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) ``` ::: ## Creating a Tibble from Vectors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(10, 20, 30, 40) y <- x * 2 - 4 y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 16 36 56 76 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} my_tibble <- tibble(x, y) my_tibble ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 x y 1 10 16 2 20 36 3 30 56 4 40 76 ``` ::: ::: ## Tibbles Can Mix Types ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} first_names <- c("Adam", "Billy", "Caitlyn", "Debra") age_years <- c(12, 13, 10, NA) guests <- tibble(first_names, age_years) guests ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 first_names age_years 1 Adam 12 2 Billy 13 3 Caitlyn 10 4 Debra NA ``` ::: ::: ::: aside *Note.* Look at the `` and `` labels --- the tibble tracks each column's type, and prints `NA` where a value is missing. ::: ## Building the Vectors Inline ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gradebook <- tibble( grade = c(95, 83, 90, 76), letter = c("a", "b", "a-", "c") ) gradebook ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 2 grade letter 1 95 a 2 83 b 3 90 a- 4 76 c ``` ::: ::: ## Pitfall: Columns Must Be the Same Length ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(y = c(1, 2, 3), x = c("a", "b")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `tibble()`: ! Tibble columns must have compatible sizes. • Size 3: Existing data. • Size 2: Column `x`. ℹ Only values of size one are recycled. ``` ::: ::: ## Extracting a Column with $ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mytibble <- tibble(x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), y = "test") mytibble$x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 4 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mytibble$y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "test" "test" "test" "test" "test" ``` ::: ::: ::: aside *Note.* `y` was a single value, so it was recycled down the whole column. Length one is the one length that is allowed to differ. ::: ## Pitfall: A Column That Does Not Exist ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mytibble$z ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `z`. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` NULL ``` ::: ::: ::: aside *Note.* This is [not]{.b} an error. You get `NULL` and a warning, so a typo in a column name can flow silently into the rest of your code. ::: ## Getting Information About a Tibble ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Rows and columns dim(gradebook) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Column names colnames(gradebook) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "grade" "letter" ``` ::: ::: ## Data Files {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - Data is usually stored in [data files]{.b .green} - Importing files into R is called [reading]{.b .blue} - Exporting files from R is called [writing]{.b .blue} ::: {.fragment .mt1} - A convenient data file type is a CSV - This stands for [comma-separated values]{.b .green} - A CSV file is easy to share with other people ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - The [tidyverse]{.b .green} package can read/write CSVs - Other packages can read/write other types (e.g., *readxl*, *haven*, *rio*, *googlesheets4*) ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/freight_ship.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Getting a Data File {.fs70} - Download [`gradebook.csv`]{.b .blue} from the course website into your project folder ::: {.fragment .mt1} - You can see it in the [Extras pane > Files tab]{.b .green} - And open it in another program, such as Excel ::: ## Reading in a Data File ::: {.cell replace_path='["../../data/",""]'} ```{.r .cell-code} old_gradebook <- read_csv("../../data/gradebook.csv") old_gradebook ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 id grade 1 123 A 2 456 B 3 789 ? ``` ::: ::: ::: aside *Note.* `read_csv()` examines each column and guesses its type. You can state the types yourself, but that is more advanced. ::: ## Pitfall: Missing Values in Disguise One student's grade is recorded as `?`. R has no idea that means "missing" --- unless we say so with `na = "?"`, it stays a real value that pollutes the column. ::: {.cell replace_path='["../../data/",""]'} ```{.r .cell-code} old_gradebook <- read_csv("../../data/gradebook.csv", na = "?") old_gradebook ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 2 id grade 1 123 A 2 456 B 3 789 ``` ::: ::: ## Other Kinds of Data File {.fs70} - [readxl]{.b .blue} and [googlesheets4]{.b .blue} --- spreadsheets ::: {.fragment .mt1} - [haven]{.b .blue} --- files from SPSS, SAS, and STATA ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - [rio]{.b .blue} --- tries to detect the type and read in anything ::: # Data Exploration ## Data Verification {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - It's always a good idea to start with [verification]{.b .blue} ::: {.fragment .mt1} - Check that your variables are the [correct type]{.b .green} - Configure your [factors]{.b .green}' levels and labels - Establish ordinal factors' ordering - Explicitly set your [missing values]{.b .green} to NA ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - Check variables' [extrema]{.b .green} and [distributions]{.b .green} - Check for erroneous and outlying values - Check the shape of continuous distributions - Check the overlap of categorical levels ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/avatar_search.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Reading in the Raw Penguins Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(easystats) ``` ::: ::: {.cell replace_path='["../../data/",""]'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins <- read_csv("../../data/penguins0.csv") penguins ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 344 × 8 species island bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex year 1 1 3 39.1 18.7 181 3750 2 2007 2 1 3 39.5 17.4 186 3800 1 2007 3 1 3 40.3 18 195 3250 1 2007 4 1 3 NA NA NA NA NA 2007 5 1 3 36.7 19.3 193 3450 1 2007 6 1 3 39.3 20.6 190 3650 2 2007 7 1 3 38.9 17.8 181 3625 1 2007 8 1 3 39.2 19.6 195 4675 2 2007 9 1 3 34.1 18.1 193 3475 NA 2007 10 1 3 42 20.2 190 4250 NA 2007 # ℹ 334 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: aside *Note.* `species`, `island`, and `sex` arrived as numbers. They are categories, and R does not know that yet. ::: ## Configuring the Factors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins$species <- factor(penguins$species, levels = c(1, 2, 3), labels = c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo")) penguins$island <- factor(penguins$island, levels = c(1, 2, 3), labels = c("Biscoe", "Dream", "Torgersen")) penguins$sex <- factor(penguins$sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("female", "male")) ``` ::: ## The Configured Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 344 × 8 species island bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass sex year 1 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181 3750 male 2007 2 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 17.4 186 3800 female 2007 3 Adelie Torgersen 40.3 18 195 3250 female 2007 4 Adelie Torgersen NA NA NA NA 2007 5 Adelie Torgersen 36.7 19.3 193 3450 female 2007 6 Adelie Torgersen 39.3 20.6 190 3650 male 2007 7 Adelie Torgersen 38.9 17.8 181 3625 female 2007 8 Adelie Torgersen 39.2 19.6 195 4675 male 2007 9 Adelie Torgersen 34.1 18.1 193 3475 2007 10 Adelie Torgersen 42 20.2 190 4250 2007 # ℹ 334 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: aside *Note.* Those three columns now print as `` with readable values. Save the cleaned version with `write_csv(penguins, "penguins.csv")` so you never redo this. ::: ## Checking the Summary for Problems ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(penguins) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` species island bill_len bill_dep Adelie :152 Biscoe :168 Min. :32.10 Min. :13.10 Chinstrap: 68 Dream :124 1st Qu.:39.23 1st Qu.:15.60 Gentoo :124 Torgersen: 52 Median :44.45 Median :17.30 Mean :43.92 Mean :17.15 3rd Qu.:48.50 3rd Qu.:18.70 Max. :59.60 Max. :21.50 NAs :2 NAs :2 flipper_len body_mass sex year Min. :172.0 Min. :2700 female:165 Min. :2007 1st Qu.:190.0 1st Qu.:3550 male :168 1st Qu.:2007 Median :197.0 Median :4050 NAs : 11 Median :2008 Mean :200.9 Mean :4202 Mean :2008 3rd Qu.:213.0 3rd Qu.:4750 3rd Qu.:2009 Max. :231.0 Max. :6300 Max. :2009 NAs :2 NAs :2 ``` ::: ::: ::: aside *Note.* Read the `NA` counts: 2 penguins were never measured and 11 (including those 2) were never sexed. Real data has holes, and this is where you find them. ::: ## Describing One Continuous Variable ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} describe_distribution(penguins, body_mass) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Variable | Mean | SD | IQR | Range | Skewness ---------------------------------------------------------------------- body_mass | 4201.75 | 801.95 | 1206.25 | [2700.00, 6300.00] | 0.47 Variable | Kurtosis | n | n_Missing -------------------------------------- body_mass | -0.72 | 342 | 2 ``` ::: ::: ## Describing All of Them at Once ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} describe_distribution(penguins) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Variable | Mean | SD | IQR | Range | Skewness ------------------------------------------------------------------------ bill_len | 43.92 | 5.46 | 9.30 | [32.10, 59.60] | 0.05 bill_dep | 17.15 | 1.97 | 3.12 | [13.10, 21.50] | -0.14 flipper_len | 200.92 | 14.06 | 23.25 | [172.00, 231.00] | 0.35 body_mass | 4201.75 | 801.95 | 1206.25 | [2700.00, 6300.00] | 0.47 year | 2008.03 | 0.82 | 2.00 | [2007.00, 2009.00] | -0.05 Variable | Kurtosis | n | n_Missing ---------------------------------------- bill_len | -0.88 | 342 | 2 bill_dep | -0.91 | 342 | 2 flipper_len | -0.98 | 342 | 2 body_mass | -0.72 | 342 | 2 year | -1.50 | 344 | 0 ``` ::: ::: ## Tabulating One Factor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data_tabulate(penguins, species) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` species (species) # total N=344 valid N=344 Value | N | Raw % | Valid % | Cumulative % ----------+-----+-------+---------+------------- Adelie | 152 | 44.19 | 44.19 | 44.19 Chinstrap | 68 | 19.77 | 19.77 | 63.95 Gentoo | 124 | 36.05 | 36.05 | 100.00 | 0 | 0.00 | | ``` ::: ::: ## Tabulating Every Factor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data_tabulate(penguins, is.factor) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` species (species) # total N=344 valid N=344 Value | N | Raw % | Valid % | Cumulative % ----------+-----+-------+---------+------------- Adelie | 152 | 44.19 | 44.19 | 44.19 Chinstrap | 68 | 19.77 | 19.77 | 63.95 Gentoo | 124 | 36.05 | 36.05 | 100.00 | 0 | 0.00 | | island (island) # total N=344 valid N=344 Value | N | Raw % | Valid % | Cumulative % ----------+-----+-------+---------+------------- Biscoe | 168 | 48.84 | 48.84 | 48.84 Dream | 124 | 36.05 | 36.05 | 84.88 Torgersen | 52 | 15.12 | 15.12 | 100.00 | 0 | 0.00 | | sex (sex) # total N=344 valid N=333 Value | N | Raw % | Valid % | Cumulative % -------+-----+-------+---------+------------- female | 165 | 47.97 | 49.55 | 49.55 male | 168 | 48.84 | 50.45 | 100.00 | 11 | 3.20 | | ``` ::: ::: ## Data Visualization {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - [Variable distributions]{.b .blue} are critical in data analysis - What are the most and least [common values]{.b .green}? - What are the [extrema]{.b .green} (min and max values)? - Are there any [outliers]{.b .green} or impossible values? - How much [spread]{.b .green} is there in the variable? - What [shape]{.b .green} does the distribution take? ::: {.fragment .mt1} - Distributions describe a single variable's [variation]{.b .green} - We also visualize many variables' [covariation]{.b .blue} ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/dice.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Loading the Cleaned Data ::: {.cell replace_path='["../../data/",""]'} ```{.r .cell-code} penguins <- read_csv("../../data/penguins.csv") ``` ::: ## Variation of a Factor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = species, data = penguins, geom = "bar") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: `qplot()` was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: aside *Note.* `qplot()` warns that it is deprecated. It still works and we will keep using it here; the warning appears once per session, not once per plot. ::: ## Variation of Another Factor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = island, data = penguins, geom = "bar") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Variation of a Continuous Variable ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = flipper_len, data = penguins, geom = "histogram") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The Same Variable as a Boxplot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = flipper_len, data = penguins, geom = "boxplot") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Body Mass as a Histogram ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = body_mass, data = penguins, geom = "histogram") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Body Mass as a Boxplot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = body_mass, data = penguins, geom = "boxplot") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Covariation of Two Continuous Variables ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, data = penguins, geom = "point") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Covariation of Two Factors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = species, y = island, data = penguins, geom = "jitter") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The Same Pair as Stacked Bars ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = species, fill = island, data = penguins, geom = "bar") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## A Factor and a Continuous Variable ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = body_mass, y = species, data = penguins, geom = "boxplot") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The Same Pair as Violins ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qplot(x = body_mass, y = species, data = penguins, geom = "violin") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){width=672} ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
